prompt.context: Your client is a production studio looking to release its new film, Leo vs. The Space Invaders, in the next year. The film is the fifth movie in the franchise, and the studio is deciding whether to sell exclusive rights to a 3rd party streaming service or stick with the original plan and release the film in theaters.
prompt.question: How would you advise the CEO: should the studio sell exclusive streaming rights or release the film in theaters?

clarifying_info.a: An American film studio that has released several blockbusters in the Leo franchise. The first three movies made over $200M each in the box office, but the fourth finished with only $50M in revenue due to a global pandemic.

clarifying_info.q: What market are we focused on?
clarifying_info.a: Only the U.S. market for this release. It is currently 2021. Theaters are opening back up after the global pandemic; some people may be hesitant to go, but many are excited to return to cinema. There were 5,000 theaters in the U.S. as of 2019.

clarifying_info.q: What is the streaming service offering?
clarifying_info.a: There are 15 main streaming services. The one with the most subscribers is offering $150M for exclusive streaming rights of the film.
We will discuss those later (costs are shown in Exhibit 2).

clarifying_info.q: What about DVD or digital download sales?
clarifying_info.a: That is a good question, but we are more concerned about short-term profitability for now.

exhibits.title: Revenue for previous 4 Leo films vs. total US box office
exhibits.shows: A dual-axis chart showing Leo franchise film revenue (bar chart, left axis in USD $M) and total U.S. box office revenue (line chart, right axis in USD $B) for the years 2014, 2017, 2019, and 2020.

exhibits.title: Costs for each type of release
exhibits.shows: A table comparing production cost, marketing cost, and distribution fee for two options: Release in Theaters vs. Sell to Streaming Service.

framework: Revenue: (Theater) ticket price, volume of ticket-buyers, weeks in theaters, month/seasonality of release; (Streaming) flat fee vs. per-view payment from streaming service
Costs Fixed: marketing spend under each format, actor/director compensation changes, any contract-breach fee for switching to streaming
Costs Variable: theater revenue-share percentage, film shipping costs
Risks (Streaming): theater chain retaliation, reputation risk, future contract difficulty with talent who prefer theaters
Risks (Theater Release): declining attendance as streaming grows, pandemic-related hesitancy depressing actual attendance
Benchmarking: use past Leo franchise performance as a baseline for expected theater revenue

questions.prompt: Analyze Exhibit 1. What do the Leo franchise revenue figures show relative to total U.S. box office?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate Leo films as a % of total U.S. box office each year, observe an upward trend (with 2020 as a pandemic outlier), and question whether 2020 represents the new normal or a one-time anomaly. Candidate should then ask for 2022 theater projections.

math.setup: Leo revenue / U.S. box office each year; then project 2022 box office using provided data: 80% of 5,000 theaters open, 100 seats/screen, 20 showtimes/theater/day, $10/ticket, 50% occupancy on weekends and 25% on weekdays.
steps: Average Leo share ≈ 2.5% of U.S. box office
Daily revenue capacity = 4,000 theaters × 20 showtimes × 100 seats × $10 = $80M/day
math.answer: Estimated 2022 theater revenue for Leo vs. The Space Invaders ≈ $225M

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate expected profit for each release option and compare them.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the cost structure from Exhibit 2 to the $225M estimated theater revenue and the $150M streaming offer, arriving at nearly identical profits (~$105M vs. ~$100M). Key insight: theater profit is an estimate with both upside and downside risk, while streaming profit is fixed. Candidate should discuss upside/downside scenarios.

math.setup: Theater: Revenue - Distribution Fee - Production - Marketing. Streaming: Streaming fee - Production.
math.answer: Theater profit ≈ $105M (estimated); Streaming profit = $100M (fixed). The gap is minimal at ~$5M.

brainstorming.prompt: What else can the production company do to maximize its profit potential?

categories.name: Revenue – Theater + Streaming Hybrid
ideas: Structure a deal to release in theaters for a short window first, then sell exclusive streaming rights afterward to capture revenue from both channels.
Negotiate with multiple streaming services to create a bidding war and drive up the offer price above $150M.

categories.name: Revenue – Ancillary
ideas: Explore merchandising arrangements to retain a share of merchandise revenue even if the film rights are sold to a streaming service.
Investigate digital download or DVD rights retention if the streaming deal only covers a defined exclusivity window.

categories.name: Costs
ideas: Re-negotiate the theater distribution fee (currently 20%) to improve theater-release profitability.
Partner with another production company to co-finance production costs in exchange for future revenue sharing or co-production deals.

recommendation: Either theater release or streaming sale can be justified given the nearly identical expected profit (~$105M theater vs. $100M streaming).
If risk tolerance is low or market uncertainty around post-pandemic attendance remains high, selling to the streaming service ($100M fixed) is the safer choice.

If the studio is confident consumers will return to theaters and wants to preserve brand/franchise relationships with theater chains, a theatrical release is preferred with $5M higher expected upside.
risks: Streaming risks: loss of future DVD/digital sales revenue; reputation risk from departing from traditional theatrical release; angering theater chains and weakening future negotiating leverage; higher piracy risk for streamed content.

Theater risks: profit is only an estimate — if attendance does not recover as projected (new pandemic variant, consumer preference shift), actual revenue could be significantly below $225M, erasing the $5M advantage.
next_steps: Have legal review whether existing distribution agreements can be renegotiated to lower the 20% theater distribution fee.
Survey target audiences to gauge post-pandemic preference for theater vs. streaming viewing.
Approach other streaming services to test whether a higher bid than $150M is achievable before committing to either option.
